R07-C-01: Few things in a museum are read as often, or looked at as little, as the wall label. Visitors approaching a painting frequently read the small panel beside it first, glance at the picture to confirm what they have been told, and move on. Curators have noticed this pattern for a long time, and it has produced two opposite reactions. One camp argues that labels should be shortened or removed altogether, so that the visitor is thrown back onto the object. The other argues that labels should be expanded, written in friendlier language and supplemented with audio guides and screens, since a public that does not know what it is looking at cannot be expected to care. Both reactions treat the label as though its only variable were quantity. The purist assumes that less text means more looking, but a visitor confronted by an unexplained altarpiece does not usually begin to look harder; more often she feels excluded and walks faster. The expansionist assumes that more text means more understanding, yet a long label that rehearses the artist's biography, the patron's family and the painting's later owners gives the visitor a great deal to know and very little to see. In each case the label is imagined as a container of facts, and the only argument is over how full the container should be. A better question is what the label asks the visitor to do. A label can close a picture, by telling the viewer what it means, or it can open it, by directing attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself. Compare two sentences about the same imagined portrait. The first says that the sitter was a wealthy merchant who commissioned the work to celebrate his marriage. The second says that the merchant's left hand rests on a ledger while his right holds his wife's glove, and invites the reader to decide which hand the painter has lit more brightly. The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking. None of this means that historical information is a distraction. A viewer who does not know that a certain blue, ground from a semi-precious stone, was once among the costliest materials a painter could buy will miss part of what a patron was displaying when he asked for a sky full of it, and no amount of attentive looking will supply that fact. The point is that information earns its place on the wall when it changes what the visitor notices. Facts that merely sit beside the object, however accurate, belong in the catalogue, where they can be read at leisure by those who want them. The wall is too valuable, and the visitor's attention too brief, to be spent on anything else.
R07-C-02: When a town decides to honour someone or something in public, its first instinct is usually to reach for bronze and stone. Durability is treated as a measure of respect: a statue meant to last for centuries seems to say more than a banner meant to last for a week. Yet the history of public art suggests that permanence is less a virtue than a wager, and frequently a losing one. A monument fixes one generation's judgement in a material that will outlast the judgement itself. Within a few decades the figure on the plinth may be unrecognised by most passers-by, and within a century it may be the cause of a quarrel its makers could not have imagined. The problem is not that later generations are fickle. It is that a permanent work is designed to end discussion rather than to take part in it. Once installed, it asks only to be accepted; there is no procedure built into it for being reconsidered. When disagreement finally arrives, it therefore arrives as a crisis, with petitions, counter-petitions and arguments over whether removal amounts to erasing history. A city that had expected its public art to change would face no such crisis, because it would already possess a habit of revisiting what stands in its squares. Temporary works offer one way of building that habit. A plinth that hosts a different commission every year or two, a sculpture placed in a park for a single season, a mural painted on the understanding that it will be painted over: each of these makes public art an occasion rather than a verdict. People argue about the new piece, grow fond of it or feel relieved to see it go, and in doing so they practise exactly the kind of collective judgement that a permanent statue forecloses. The work matters less as an object than as the conversation it starts. This argument has limits, and they should be stated. Temporary art can slide into novelty for its own sake, a rotating series of spectacles chosen to attract visitors rather than to say anything. And some public works aim at permanence for good reason: a memorial to the dead of a war or a disaster is meant to resist the passing of time, because forgetting is precisely the danger it guards against. The case against bronze is not a case against all lasting memorials. It is a case against the assumption that whatever a public wishes to honour must be honoured in a form that can never be questioned without a fight.
R07-C-03: Arguments about the cleaning of old paintings tend to repeat themselves with remarkable fidelity. A famous canvas is cleaned; the removal of darkened varnish reveals colours far brighter than anyone living has seen on it; and two parties form at once. One celebrates the recovery of what the painter actually intended, a picture freed from centuries of grime. The other mourns the loss of a mellow harmony that generations had loved, and suspects that the cleaners, in their zeal, have removed not only dirt but the delicate final glazes with which the painter softened his effects. It is tempting to treat this as a contest between truth and sentiment, with the cleaners on the side of truth. There is something to this. Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age, and a sky that now looks olive may well have been painted as a clear blue; to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision. Cleaning has repeatedly shown that painters long thought murky were in fact bold colourists, and no honest account of the debate can pretend otherwise. Yet the cleaners' strongest claim, that they return the painting to its original state, is harder to sustain than it sounds. Pigments themselves change: some blues fade, some greens turn brown, some reds lose their glazes to light long before any restorer arrives. Removing the varnish from such a picture does not take it back to the day it left the studio; it produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw. The bright painting revealed by cleaning may therefore be no closer to the original than the dark one it replaced, only differently distant from it. What follows is not that cleaning should stop, but that it should be described honestly. Every restoration is a judgement about which of a painting's many histories to favour, and judgements can be wrong. The responsible course is to make such judgements in ways that can be undone where possible, to record exactly what has been removed and why, and to abandon the language of revelation in favour of the language of interpretation. A restorer who says 'this is what the painter meant' claims more than any evidence can give; one who says 'this is our best reading, and here is how we reached it' claims only what the craft can support.
R07-C-04: Discussion of whether photographs can be trusted has long been dominated by the fear of manipulation. Early critics worried about staged scenes and retouched negatives; later ones about software that can add a figure to a crowd or remove one from a podium without leaving a trace visible to the eye. These worries are reasonable, and the tools that prompt them have become more powerful. But they direct attention to the least interesting way in which a photograph can mislead, and in doing so they leave the more ordinary and more pervasive problem almost untouched. Consider an unaltered photograph of a crowded square taken during a demonstration. Every figure in it was really there, standing exactly where the picture shows. The image is, in the narrow sense, entirely truthful. Yet it cannot tell us whether the square was full or whether the photographer stood at the one corner where people had gathered; whether the moment captured was typical of the afternoon or its single tense minute; whether the raised fists at the front belonged to protesters or to the counter-demonstration across the road. A photograph is accurate about what falls inside its frame and wholly silent about what falls outside it, and the frame is chosen by someone. This is why the manipulation debate can produce a false sense of security. A viewer who has learned to check for doctored pixels may conclude that an image which passes the check is reliable, when the check has said nothing about selection, timing or framing. An honest photograph can support a dishonest story as easily as a forged one can, and often more easily, since it will survive the very scrutiny that exposes a forgery. None of this makes photographs worthless as evidence. It means that their evidential value lies less in the single image than in its surroundings: the caption that states when and where it was taken, the other frames from the same roll or memory card, the identity and record of the person who took it, the existence of independent pictures of the same event. A photograph considered alone is a fragment that can be fitted into many stories. A photograph considered with these supports begins to narrow the stories it can serve. The question to ask of an image, then, is not only whether it has been altered but what would have to be true of everything around it for it to mean what it is said to mean.
R07-C-05: When a painting sells at auction for a sum that would fund a hospital, two responses compete for the headlines. The first treats the price as a verdict: the market, pooling the judgements of many informed buyers, has declared this one of the most important works of its kind. The second treats it as a scandal: the sum has nothing to do with art and everything to do with vanity, speculation and the search for places to park wealth. Each response captures something, but both share a mistaken premise, which is that the price is either a measure of artistic value or a measure of nothing at all. A price measures what someone will pay to own a thing, and owning a painting is not the same as valuing it as a painting. The buyer acquires an object that is unique, that cannot be reproduced without losing the very property being purchased, and that carries a name capable of conferring distinction on whoever holds it. Each of these features has a market logic of its own. Scarcity helps explain why a minor work by a celebrated painter can outsell a masterpiece by an obscure one; the name explains why a newly accepted attribution can multiply a canvas's price overnight without a single brushstroke changing. In neither case has anyone's experience of looking at the picture altered. This does not mean that prices float free of critical judgement. Over long periods, the artists whom critics, historians and museums take seriously tend also to be the ones whose works command high prices, and it would be perverse to call this coincidence. But the connection runs largely through reputation rather than through the works themselves: esteem builds a name, the name creates demand, and demand sets the price. The market thus registers critical judgement at second hand, much as a credit rating registers a company's prospects without being the same thing as its earnings. The real danger lies in the return journey. Once prices are reported as verdicts, they begin to shape the judgements they supposedly reflect. Visitors crowd around the record-breaking canvas while the room beside it stands empty; institutions hesitate to show or lend works whose insurance values have become unmanageable; young artists learn which styles sell. A measure of ownership, mistaken for a measure of worth, ends by teaching people what to look at. Resisting that confusion requires nothing more radical than remembering what a price is the price of.
R07-C-06: Suppose a painting has hung for decades in a museum, admired by critics and loved by visitors, and is then shown beyond doubt to be a forgery. Nothing about the canvas has changed: its colours and its composition are exactly as they were, and the pleasure that thousands took in it was genuine pleasure, not a misunderstanding awaiting correction. Yet the picture is taken down, its value collapses, and the critics who praised it are embarrassed. If what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it, this reaction looks irrational, a triumph of the label over the eye. Two familiar explanations are offered, and neither is adequate. The first says the reaction is mere snobbery: we cared about the famous name, not the picture, and the forgery has simply exposed the fact. There is truth here, since much of the fall in price reflects nothing loftier than the loss of a signature that could be resold. But the explanation proves too much; it implies that anyone who minds about the difference is a snob, including the scrupulous historian with no money at stake. The second says that the forgery must differ visibly after all, and that trained eyes, once alerted, can see its deadness. Sometimes this is so; yet the deadness is usually perceived only after the verdict is known, and a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory. A more promising account begins from the thought that we value paintings not only as arrangements of colour but also as achievements. To admire a picture fully is partly to admire what was done in making it: a problem of light or space confronted at a particular moment, with the means then available, by someone who did not know how it would turn out. The forger faces a different problem, that of producing something that will pass as the solution to the first. The two canvases may look alike, but they answer different questions, and the exposure tells us that the question we thought we were admiring an answer to was never asked by this canvas at all. This view has a cost, and it should be admitted. It makes part of a painting's value depend on facts that cannot be seen in it, and so concedes that looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation. It also allows that a forgery may be a considerable achievement of its own kind, as a feat of imitation, without ranking it beside what it imitates. But the cost seems worth paying, because the alternative is to hold that the history of art could be rewritten, without loss, by anyone with a sufficiently skilful hand.
R07-C-07: We tend to judge a portrait by asking whether it captures the person. A good portrait, on this view, reveals something of the sitter's inner life: a habit of mind, a private sorrow, the particular way one face differs from all others. Measured against this standard, many older portraits seem stiff and oddly impersonal. Rows of nobles stand in nearly identical poses, their faces composed into the same calm, their individuality apparently buried beneath velvet and armour. It is easy to conclude that their painters were trying to capture the person and largely failing. That conclusion mistakes what such portraits were for. For much of the history of European portraiture, and of several other traditions, the purpose of a commissioned portrait was less to record a personality than to establish a position. The sitter appeared as a holder of office, an heir, a bride, the head of a house. Costume, setting and objects carried meanings that contemporaries could read: the chain of a civic office, a dog standing for fidelity, a column suggesting constancy, a distant estate glimpsed through a window. A portrait of this kind was closer to a document than to a confession. Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type, since what the patron wished to have recorded was precisely the type he had come to occupy. A contemporary who knew the conventions could read an entire biography of rank in a single canvas, whereas a modern viewer expecting the revelation of a character finds only an inventory of possessions. Likeness was not irrelevant. Families wanted to know what an absent bride looked like, and painters could be criticised for flattering too much or too little. But likeness served the larger purpose rather than defining it. A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role. The expectation that a portrait should instead expose the sitter, catching him off guard or revealing what he might prefer to hide, belongs to a later and narrower moment in the genre's history. Where an older portrait does strike modern eyes as startlingly intimate, it is worth asking whether it was made for a public hall or for a private room, since the obligations of display weighed very differently in the two settings. Several changes made that expectation possible. The growth of a buying public outside courts and great houses created sitters with no office to display. New ideas about the self encouraged the belief that a person's truth lay within rather than in his station. And when photography arrived in the nineteenth century, it soon took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply. The psychological portrait, in other words, is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms. To say this is not to claim that the older portraits had no inner life, or that modern ones are free of display. A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions, and a present-day portrait of a company chairman, with its carefully chosen office and posture, documents a position as surely as any court painting did. The point is only that we should judge a portrait by the question it was asked to answer. Faulting a court painter for failing to reveal a soul is like faulting a map for failing to be a landscape painting.
R07-C-08: Anyone who watches visitors in a busy gallery will notice how briefly most pictures are looked at. A few seconds for the image, a little longer for the label, and the visitor moves on. In response, many museums now promote what is sometimes called slow looking: sessions in which participants are invited to sit before a single work for a quarter of an hour or more, noting whatever comes to their attention. The premise is simple and attractive. We miss what is in paintings because we do not give them time, and if we gave them time, they would show us more. The practice has real merits, and its critics should concede them. It interrupts the habit, encouraged by crowded rooms and handheld screens, of treating a picture as something to be recognised and ticked off. It gives permission to stay, which many visitors seem to need. And it does sometimes yield discoveries: a figure in the background that had gone unnoticed, a repeated colour that ties distant parts of the canvas together. But the premise behind it, that duration by itself turns into perception, is weaker than it looks. Fifteen minutes in front of a canvas can be fifteen minutes of reverie, of thinking about lunch, or of staring with growing unease at a surface that refuses to become interesting. Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it. What turns time into seeing is a question. The art historian who notices in a moment that the light in a landscape falls from two directions does not see faster because her eyes are better; she sees because she has learned to ask where the light comes from, and the painting answers. Expertise, in this sense, is a stock of questions that direct the eye, questions that are not mysterious endowments but are acquired, often laboriously, through the comparison of many works, and that can therefore in principle be taught. This explains why experts often see in seconds what a patient beginner misses in an hour. The beginner is not looking less; he is looking without a question, and an unguided gaze tends to settle on whatever is largest, brightest or most familiar. Yet the expert's advantage carries a risk of its own, and here the advocates of slow looking have a point that their own premise obscures. A stock of questions is also a stock of expectations. The historian who knows what to look for in a painting of a certain school may stop looking once she has found it, filing the picture under its category and failing to notice what does not fit. Questions direct the eye, but they also tell it where it need not go. Some of the most valuable observations a viewer can make come from setting expertise aside long enough to be surprised, and slow looking at its best is precisely a technique for producing that suspension. The two halves of the matter therefore need each other. Time without questions drifts; questions without time confirm what they expected. Neither ingredient is dispensable, and neither, taken in isolation, is sufficient for the kind of perception that the advocates of slow looking rightly prize. The most useful practice is neither the patient blankness that slow looking sometimes encourages nor the quick classification that expertise permits, but an alternation between them: a period of asking, a period of letting the asking lapse, and a return to the picture to see whether it has said something the questions did not predict.
